name: Columba
knownFor: Irish monk who sailed to Britain on pilgrimage for Christ, founded the monastery on Iona, and in Bede's account turned the northern Picts to the faith.
dates: Sailed to Britain in his forty-second year, two years after the battle of Cooldrevny, in Adomnán's words: 563 in Wentworth Huyshe's reckoning, 565 in Bede's. Huyshe gives his years as 521 to 597; Bede says he died at seventy-seven
place: Ireland by birth; Iona, from which he went among the Picts
role: Monk; founder and abbot of Iona

traces: Bede says many monasteries in Britain and Ireland had their beginning through his disciples from Iona and from the house he built in Ireland, the Field of Oaks, and that the Iona house was the chief of them all.
Bede says the abbot of Iona, a priest, ruled the whole province, even its bishops, after the example of Columba, who was a priest and monk and not a bishop.
remembered: Bede calls him a famous priest and abbot, a monk by habit and life, and says he left successors known for their love of God and their keeping of the monastic rule.
Adomnán says his name reached beyond Ireland and Britain to Spain, Gaul, Italy and Rome itself.

At the synod Bede places at Streaneshalch, Whitby, the Irish party called him their most reverend Father Columba; Wilfrid granted he might be a holy man and asked whether he could be preferred to Peter.

uncertain: His life comes from Adomnán, abbot of Iona, whose Life Wentworth Huyshe places between 679 and 704; Huyshe says Adomnán was born twenty-seven years after Columba died. Adomnán says he wrote from older writings and from what faithful old men told him. The Life is a book of prophecies, wonders and visions, and his sayings in it are Adomnán's report.

The year he came to Britain. Adomnán gives his forty-second year, two years after the battle of Cooldrevny; Huyshe dates the battle to 561 and the voyage to 563. Bede gives 565, in the ninth year of Bridius, king of the Picts.

His years and age. Huyshe gives 521 to 597. Bede says he died at seventy-seven, about thirty-two years after he came to Britain. The Middle Irish Life in the Book of Lismore gives seventy-seven years and forty-five in Scotland. An Old Irish Life that Huyshe quotes says he was forty-two when he went and thirty-four years in Alba. Whitley Stokes reports that Bishop William Reeves chose 521 for his birth from among 517, 521 and 523.

Why he left Ireland. Huyshe says later tradition tied his going to the battle of Cooldrevny and a penance; he calls these legends, and says the Old Irish Life tells only of a pilgrimage long resolved. Adomnán names the battle only to give the date.
Who gave him Iona. Bede says the Picts gave him the island. Huyshe says the Irish annals name Conall, son of Comgill, king of the Irish of Dalriada in Britain; no annals are held.

The day of his death. Adomnán puts it in the night after a Saturday, soon after a day in May when he blessed the island. The Book of Lismore Life says the night of Pentecost Sunday. Huyshe gives his feast as 9 June.

Later tradition credits him with poems and hymns. For the Latin hymn Altus Prosator, Huyshe reports the Marquess of Bute's view that the ascription rests on an apparently unbroken tradition and seems open to no serious doubt. The Library holds only Huyshe's English of some stanzas and poems.
